name: Low German (Plattdeutsch)
notes: Low German (Plattdeutsch / Nedderdütsch), encoded for the SASS orthography of Northern Low Saxon (Nordniedersächsisch), the most widely used Low German spelling. Descended from Old Saxon — NOT from Old High German — and it did not undergo the High German consonant shift: maken vs. German machen, water vs. German Wasser. There is no ⟨pf⟩ for that reason. VOWEL LENGTH is written three ways and no other (SASS §§3–5): a Dehnungs-h in words whose High German cognate has one (§3: gahn, mehr); doubled ⟨aa ää ee oo öö uu üü yy⟩ in a closed syllable (§5 I: Aal, Straat, Schüün, gröön); and ⟨ie⟩ for long i (§12: Ies, hier, frie). In an OPEN syllable length is simply not written (§4 I: sche-ten, grö-ne, Se-len, and the monosyllables bi, du, he, se, na, to, so, wo), which is what the NDS_OPEN_SYLLABLE_* and NDS_OPEN_FINAL_* rules restore. LONG A IS DARK: it ranges from [ɔː] to [oː] and is written ⟨a/aa/ah⟩ (SASS §9; SASS-Grammatik 1.1.4.1 "Langes a" gives kamen, Straat, Hahn). VOWEL SHORTNESS is written by doubling the FOLLOWING consonant (§6: Katt, Kopp, seggen, tappen) — the doubled letter marks the vowel, not a long consonant, hence collapse_geminates. UNSTRESSED SYLLABLES: ⟨-en⟩ loses its e and is spoken as a syllabic nasal, ⟨-el⟩ as a syllabic lateral, and ⟨-er⟩ as [ɐ] (SASS §§23/27; SASS-Grammatik 1.1.4.5: Gavel [ɡɔːvl̩], laten [lɔːtn̩], Schöler [ʃøːlɐ]). Stress is word-initial (Lindow et al. 1998:30, reported in Prehn 2012 §4.1). R: the onset rhotic is apical — a trill or tap — with uvular [ʁ] a German-contact variant, so all three stay in the lattice; post-vocalic ⟨r⟩ vocalises, "the original /r/ vocalizes to a full-fledged [a] in post-vocalic, syllable- or word-final position" (Prehn 2012 §5.1), and SASS §9 likewise speaks of a "zu a vokalisierten r". FORTIS/LENIS: a word-final lenis obstruent surfaces voiceless — Prehn 2012 argues Low German has a laryngeally unspecified lenis series whose lack of a laryngeal node allows "voicelessness in voiceless and word-final context", which subsumes the traditional final-devoicing process (Prehn 2012 ch. 3, ch. 6). G: word-initial ⟨g⟩ is [ɡ], and [ç] in Schleswig (SASS §16 I transcribes gele Georginen with [ç] throughout); word-final ⟨g⟩ is [ç/x] (§16 II: Dag, Tog, weg); intervocalic ⟨g⟩ is [ɡ] (§16 III: negen, stiegen, hoge). V/W: ⟨w⟩ is written word-initially and ⟨v⟩ elsewhere (§21: Water, Gloov, Gloven); the intervocalic v/b sound is [v] (§18). ⟨sl sm sn sp st sw⟩ are written with s whether [s] or [ʃ] is spoken (§20: slaan, snuven, spelen, stöten), so both readings stay in the lattice. Dialect diversity is real and this gold set reflects it: Westphalian and Dutch Low Saxon spellings (⟨uo iä äö ao⟩) and idiosyncratic letters (⟨â à å ë ę æ œ⟩) occur alongside SASS. Those letters are mapped to their base letter's values so that no character is silently dropped; their dialect-specific values are not asserted. ENDING "en" is [ən] at rank 1, with the syllabic nasal [n̩] carried as a lattice alternative (SASS-Grammatik 1.1.4.5; Thies 2011, gives Gavel [ɡɔːvl̩]); lattice-hole evidence for "en" (the admissibility bar in SCHEMA.md, 0-in-top-k on gold): before this entry [n̩] appeared in word_candidates 0 times in the top 5 for any of the 89 gold words ending in ⟨-en⟩, and after it 75 of those 89 carry [n̩] within the top 5 while rank 1 is unchanged; of the 161 pronunciation occurrences those 89 words carry in the gold, 95 already write [ə n] and 33 write [n̩] (5 more surface as [ŋ̩] after a velar), so the crowd-scraped convention keeps [ən] the majority reading. ordering basis for "en": rank 1 stays [ən] because that is the gold's own majority spelling-to-sound convention, not because SASS-Grammatik 1.1.4.5's "das e fällt stets aus" is wrong — it is added below rank 1 exactly as fr-FR's ⟨-ent⟩ entry defers to the base path. ENDING "er" is [ər] at rank 1, with the syllabic [ɐ] carried as a lattice alternative (SASS-Grammatik 1.1.4.5; Thies 2011, gives Schöler [ʃøːlɐ]); lattice-hole evidence for "er": before this entry [ɐ] appeared in word_candidates 0 times in the top 5 for any of the 19 gold words ending in ⟨-er⟩, and after it 15 of those 19 carry [ɐ] within the top 5 while rank 1 is unchanged. ordering basis for "er": rank 1 stays [ər] for the same reason as "en" — the crowd-scraped gold's own convention, not the prescriptive grammar, is what the base path already produces.

sources.title: SASS Plattdeutsche Schreibregeln
sources.notes: The 1956 Saß spelling rules for Northern Low Saxon, in Thies's fully documented edition. Cited here for every orthographic claim: what marks vowel length, what marks vowel shortness, and the g/v/w/s conventions.

sources.author: Thies, Heinrich
sources.title: SASS Plattdeutsche Grammatik
sources.notes: Supplies the phonetic values behind the spelling rules: long a as [ɔː]~[oː], and the syllabic -el/-en and [ɐ] of -er.

sources.author: Prehn, Maike
sources.title: Vowel quantity and the fortis-lenis distinction in North Low Saxon
sources.notes: Instrumental study of North Low Saxon quantity. Cited for post-vocalic r-vocalization and for the word-final voicelessness of lenis obstruents.

orthography_standard.name: SASS Plattdüütsche Schrievregeln
orthography_standard.notes: Agreed in 1956 for Northern Low Saxon and the most widely used Low German spelling, but not an official norm and not universal: Westphalian, Eastphalian and Dutch Low Saxon writing traditions spell the same language differently.
